headings.title: Browser read ownership and stale state

html:
Inference status and telemetry flows

The serving indicator answers whether the selected managed model is stopped, starting, ready or handling observed requests. A user-started timeline correlates request observations with GPU readings and existing backend counters. These two views share observation hooks but have different lifetimes and storage rules.

This page follows the serving-status owner, capture coordinator, request observer and token normalization. The lifecycle guide owns process changes and model bindings. The Inference manual explains the user controls.

Ownership and data paths

flowchart TD L[Published launch generations] --> S[Serving-status projection] L --> T[Timeline attribution] R[Existing model transport] --> O[Attempt observations] P[Routing preflight failures] --> O O --> S O --> T S --> B[Status API and UI invalidation] T --> C[Owner-bound capture in RAM] G[Local or remote GPU sampler] --> C M[Existing Portal backend metrics] --> C C --> A[Bounded capture pages] A --> U[Timeline browser buffer] A --> E[JSON or CSV download]

Manager startup installs the serving-status listener even when nobody has started a timeline. The timeline subscribes while captures are active and shares one GPU sampling task per participating host. Status snapshots and request callbacks use detached launch information rather than querying providers or SQLite. Starting a capture does read host registration and initiate GPU observation; it does not submit model work or change worker settings.

Captures stay in Controller memory and disappear on restart. Browser session storage retains the monitor identity and display preferences, not the collected request/GPU rows. The integrated routes use the Controller's management and login boundaries. Status, resume-last and telemetry routes are excluded from model-tool discovery. A capture belongs to its authenticated username; missing and foreign capture IDs both return 404.

One observed transport attempt

The tracing boundary binds request identity and manager ownership through context variables. Decorated JSON/text transports and the native streaming transport allocate an observer only when a listener exists at entry.

sequenceDiagram participant C as Traced caller participant T as Model transport participant O as Attempt observer participant V as Interested receivers participant H as HTTP endpoint C->>T: Invoke with request and owner context T->>O: Own a separate attempt context T->>T: Prepare and check dispatch lifetime T->>O: dispatch immediately before HTTP O->>V: Snapshot listeners and publish running row T->>H: Send model request opt Streaming output arrives H-->>T: Reasoning or actionable output T->>O: Mark first observed output once O->>V: Publish elapsed first-output time end H-->>T: Response, usage or transport failure T->>O: Collect validated usage and finish O->>V: Publish completed, failed or cancelled row T-->>C: Original result or exception

Each decorated retry has a separate attempt ID. Failure before the transport's dispatch hook emits no transport row. There is a separate diagnostic path: routing preflight can explicitly publish a failed row with preflight: true, elapsed time and no usage before any HTTP request. Consumers must not equate every recorded row with a provider request. In that path, the initial running publication precedes the preflight marker on the final row.

Rows contain timing, validated counts and routing identifiers, without prompt, response or endpoint text. Listener selection receives the client for attribution; row receivers receive shallow copies. Listener/receiver Exception failures are suppressed. Callbacks remain synchronous, so a slow callback can add latency; this is not a general guarantee against every BaseException.

Usage is normalized from recognized provider fields, preserving unknown values instead of inventing zeros. Counts must be nonnegative safe integers; durations must be finite and bounded. Cached counts above a known prompt total are discarded. First-output delay measures local receipt of streaming output. It is not provider prefill time, and ordinary JSON responses leave it unknown. Usage publishes at termination rather than on every token. Unsubscribing affects future dispatch snapshots; an already selected receiver can remain attached until completion.

Attribution and serving status

flowchart TD O[Client and request owner] --> F{Foreign manager?} F -->|Yes| X[Ignore observation] F -->|No| M{Managed identity?} M -->|Yes| G[Require matching instance and generation] M -->|No| E[Require one exact normalized endpoint match] G --> R{Ready target matched?} E --> R R -->|No| X R -->|Yes| S[Status receiver fences later generation changes] R -->|Yes| T[Timeline receiver retains original attribution] S --> A[Bounded active attempt identities] T --> C[Active captures on participating hosts]

Endpoint matching removes a trailing slash but keeps the complete base-URL path; the system does not infer identity from a port or model name. Managed identities must match the published launch generation. Timeline participation includes the serving host and the hosts of the recorded GPU placements. Verified worker UUIDs, when available, filter the configured placements; exported attribution states its source and omits the native endpoint.

The status receiver ignores duplicate terminal callbacks, disposed listeners and old generations. Launch publication removes active IDs for replaced, stopped or missing targets. It permits at most 4,096 active identities; malformed or excessive observations make the indicator unavailable. Silence alone does not time out an active identity. Timeline receivers instead retain the generation attributed at dispatch, so a late result can complete that historical row while its capture is still running. Stopping the capture rejects later writes.

The selected status target is the managed Main binding, including when that target is stopped. Without a managed Main, the fallback is the most recently successfully loaded local instance, with instance ID breaking timestamp ties. Remote-only and never-successful instances are excluded from that fallback. Helper and Vision do not replace Main in the indicator.

State precedence for the selected target is explicit:

Evidence, in precedence order Display state
Observer failed or manager closed Unknown
Stop/delete/shutdown operation, or stopping launch Stopping
Start/restart operation Starting
Service stopped or failed Stopped
Service shutting down Stopping
Service starting/restarting, or launch still starting/recovering Starting
Launch stopped or failed Stopped
Ready service and launch with endpoint Inferencing with active IDs, otherwise ready
Anything else Unknown

An active-count or target change invalidates the UI through inference.status.changed. Broker errors cannot fail the observed request. GET /status returns a no-store projection; it does not start a process.

Status refresh and explicit resume

The shared status component serves desktop, immersive and mobile Chat. Visible pages coalesce reads, refresh about every two seconds and react to broker/settings invalidations. Reads have a three-second deadline; a five-second stale timer changes the display to unknown. Generation checks discard late responses. A missing feature hides the component. Leaving or hiding the page aborts its reads and command watcher.

sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant B as Status component participant A as Management API participant M as Lifecycle manager B->>A: Read status or refresh after invalidation A-->>B: Detached selection and resume eligibility U->>B: Click stopped eligible instance B->>A: Read fresh status and confirm same selection opt Service is stopped or failed B->>A: Explicit service start with idempotency key A->>M: Enqueue lifecycle operation B->>A: Poll operation until terminal B->>A: Read status again end opt Selected instance remains stopped and eligible B->>A: POST resume-last with idempotency key A->>A: Recheck selection, conflicts and successful snapshot A->>M: Enqueue start from successful launch request B->>A: Poll operation until terminal end B->>A: Refresh resulting status

Resume-last preserves newer profile edits and starts from the last successful launch request. It reuses a matching idempotent start, rejects a changed selection, conflicting lifecycle operation, active start/stop task or missing successful snapshot, and delegates execution to the existing lifecycle worker. Startup completion remains separate from HTTP acceptance. Aborting a browser watcher does not cancel a previously accepted lifecycle operation. Other indicator states open the Inference page.

Browser read ownership and stale state

The browser component owns one pending status read. It polls approximately two seconds after a read settles, rather than assuming every request finishes on a fixed interval. A shared broker/settings invalidation advances its local epoch. If a read is pending, callers share that promise while recording demand for an immediate trailing read. The old response is discarded if its captured epoch no longer matches; the first promise can therefore resolve without the newer snapshot.

flowchart TD Trigger[Mount, visible-page return or refresh timer] --> Read[Coalesced status GET] Update[Broker or settings invalidation] --> Epoch[Advance epoch and mark dirty] Epoch --> Read Read --> Outcome[Response or three-second deadline failure] Outcome --> Fence{Still visible and current epoch?} Fence -->|No| Ignore[Discard obsolete result] Fence -->|Yes| Valid{Valid version-1 snapshot?} Valid -->|Yes| Adopt[Adopt instances, visibility and feature absence] Valid -->|No or read failure| Unknown[Unknown with cached resume disabled] Adopt --> Stale[Arm five-second stale timer] Stale -->|No newer accepted snapshot| StaleView[Render unknown without starting a read] Ignore --> Settle[Release pending read] Adopt --> Settle Unknown --> Settle Settle --> Observe{Visible and feature present?} Observe -->|No| Wait[Wait for a later explicit refresh or page return] Observe -->|Yes| Dirty{Invalidated during this read?} Dirty -->|Yes| Now[Schedule immediate trailing read] Dirty -->|No| Later[Schedule read after two seconds] Now --> Read Later --> Read

Accepted status data must use schema version 1, boolean visibility and an instance array with string identities/names, role arrays and recognized per-instance states. The display prefers a primary-role name, otherwise the first projected instance. Unknown state retains last-known names and suppresses a confident active-request count. A broker disconnect invalidates cached status and triggers a fresh read; successful HTTP polling restores the serving state without waiting for the broker to reconnect. Failed or stale reads remain unknown. These labels do not authorize startup.

Only a 404 from /status is interpreted as feature absence. It hides the control and stops routine polling; a later explicit refresh/invalidation can check again. A valid visible: false result also hides the control but does not by itself stop normal reads. Other read failures produce unknown state. Five seconds after the last accepted snapshot, the stale timer also sets unknown and clears cached resume eligibility. Refresh/deadline timers are cleared when the page is suspended.

Shared update-transport freshness is a separate signal. Any state other than connected forces unknown presentation and blocks the startup helper. A connected signal triggers reconciliation. The browser's online event requests a read; it does not itself clear the broker-disconnected flag. Conversely, an ordinary successful HTTP response cannot override that flag while the broker still reports an unavailable transport.

Explicit commands and page suspension

A stopped-instance click captures the first projected instance identity, then reads fresh status before sending any command. Both aggregate and matching-instance resume eligibility must still be true, and the matching instance must remain stopped. A selection change is rejected instead of substituting another model for that click.

If the service is stopped or failed, the component sends an explicit confirmed service start, watches its operation, then reads status again. That startup may already restore the selected instance. The component sends resume-last only if the same instance still exists, remains stopped and is eligible; it does not send a second resume simply because a prior status was stopped. If the instance is no longer stopped, the following status observation describes its actual state rather than the click handler declaring it ready.

Each POST gets a fresh idempotency key. Service start and resume-last use distinct keys, and this component does not automatically retry an uncertain write. Command requests have ten-second deadlines. Operation observation waits one second between GETs, uses a five-second deadline per GET, and requires complete with state completed for success. The watcher has no overall timeout: server lifecycle ownership remains responsible for its operation. Failure or an unconfirmed transport outcome opens a public error dialog with a link to Inference for reconciliation.

sequenceDiagram participant P as Browser page lifecycle participant B as Inference status control participant A as Management API participant O as Accepted lifecycle operation B->>A: Explicit startup POST after fresh eligibility check A-->>B: Accepted operation identity A->>O: Existing lifecycle owner executes operation par Observe the accepted operation loop While incomplete and page command remains owned B->>B: Wait one second B->>A: GET operation with five-second deadline A-->>B: Operation state and completion flag end and Page hides while the operation is pending P->>B: Page hidden or pagehide B->>B: Advance epoch and clear read/stale timers B->>B: Abort browser status read and command watcher Note over B,O: Accepted server operation is not cancelled O->>O: Continue under server lifecycle ownership end P->>B: Page visible or pageshow B->>A: Read fresh status A-->>B: Current observed state

Page suspension cancels browser HTTP/delay observation and suppresses its startup error dialog when the command controller was explicitly aborted. It sends no server cancellation. The startup helper always releases busy state and requests reconciliation; a hidden page defers that read until observation resumes. Other button states open /inference#instances. While startup is pending, ordinary navigation can still open Inference to inspect the accepted operation.

The selected browser fixtures exercise desktop/mobile duplicate clicks, service restoration without a second resume, changed selections, late response rejection and hidden/stale read behavior. Management responses and operation completion are mocked, so these checks start no real model service. Layout/theme and immersive appearance cases are outside this source-comment review.

Capture lifetime and shared sampling

The tab-local monitor owns renewal independently of the timeline chart. Starting another host first stops the current running capture. Renewal normally runs every 15 seconds while the page remains present; navigation can restore the saved identity. Page exit stops renewal rather than issuing a worker or capture-stop command.

sequenceDiagram participant U as User and monitor participant A as Capture API participant C as Capture coordinator participant S as Shared host sampler U->>A: Start capture for local or registered host A->>C: Bind authenticated owner and check session limit C->>C: Subscribe observations and start maintenance C->>S: Ensure one sampler for this active host A-->>U: Capture identity and renewal lease loop While the page renews U->>A: Renew before the 120-second lease expires A->>C: Refresh lease only if still running end alt Explicit stop U->>A: Stop capture A->>C: Freeze rows and mark running calls capture_ended else Lease expires C->>C: Stop capture during lookup or maintenance end C->>S: Cancel and join when host has no active captures Note over A,C: Retain stopped capture for ten-minute export grace C->>C: Prune expired history

There are at most eight retained sessions. A new session can replace an old stopped one; eight active sessions cause 409. Expiry cannot be reversed by renewal. Stopping marks only the observation as capture_ended; the model request may continue. Maintenance removes idle listeners and joins owned sampler tasks. Manager shutdown cancels maintenance and clears all captures.

flowchart TD C[Host has active captures] --> H{Local host?} H -->|Yes| L[Portal shared one-second GPU cache] L --> P[Bounded NVIDIA-SMI probe] H -->|No| V[Check remote metrics protocol] V -->|Supported| R[Fetch remote structured GPU sample] V -->|Unsupported| G[Availability and gap evidence] P --> N[Validate values and align sample time] R --> N N --> F[Fan out to active host captures] N -->|Missing or failed| G G --> F B[Existing Portal backend metric cache] --> D[Freshness and generation checks] D --> Q[Totals and eligible interval rates] Q --> F

The Portal sampler coalesces local GPU reads in a shielded task and reuses results for up to one second. The hardware probe bounds the command to three seconds and 64 KiB by default, parses device-wide readings, and kills/reaps its subprocess on timeout or cancellation. Missing hardware or unsupported values remain unavailable. It does not launch inference.

Remote protocol support is rechecked about every 30 seconds. Node checks use a three-second timeout and GPU requests four seconds. The Controller estimates sample time from the request midpoint, reported sample age and duration; it retains the remote timestamp separately and includes alignment uncertainty. GPU sampling runs roughly once per second and can miss short spikes. Readings include unrelated workloads. Fan percentage is the device-reported setting, not RPM.

Backend sampling reads Portal's already collected metrics; it does not send a new model or backend request. Values older than ten seconds become unavailable. Rates require fresh consecutive samples from the same generation, a positive interval no greater than ten seconds, and no observed counter reset. Backend totals include direct clients and overlap the observed Controller requests.

Bounded records and exports

flowchart TD I[Request, GPU, backend or gap update] --> S{Capture stopped?} S -->|Yes| X[Ignore late update] S -->|No| K[Replace same kind and ID] K --> N[Assign new sequence and observation time] N --> J[Require finite JSON and bounded row size] J --> F[Apply family count limits] F --> W[Apply ten-minute and eight-MiB limits] W --> B[Ordered capture buffer] B --> P[Page after cursor and optional ceiling] P --> O[Records plus continuation and gap evidence]

A capture retains at most 5,000 request records, 600 records per other family, eight MiB total and ten minutes of active observation. GPU families are per device; backend families are per instance. Oversized rows above 512 KiB become gap evidence. Replacement is an updated version of the same row and does not count as eviction. Actual eviction advances gap evidence. Pages carry at most 500 records and reserve metadata space within a one-MiB response budget; participating-instance metadata is bounded separately to eight KiB and reports truncation.

The timeline viewer keeps its own bounded browser buffer. Visible, unpaused charts poll about every second, or sooner for continuation pages. Pausing, hiding or disposing the chart stops page retrieval/rendering without ending the monitor's collection lease. The export command reads the server capture independently of the chart's filters, pause state and loaded subset.

sequenceDiagram participant U as Export command participant A as Capture API participant C as Capture buffer participant D as Browser download U->>A: Read first page after zero A->>C: Validate owner and read bounded page C-->>U: Records, latest cursor and gap evidence U->>U: Fix export ceiling to first latest cursor loop More retained records through that ceiling U->>A: Read next page with after and through cursors A->>C: Read current retained versions C-->>U: Next page and continuation U->>U: Merge within eight-MiB export buffer end U->>D: Download JSON or escaped CSV Note over U,D: Include gap, eviction and concurrent-change indicators

A fixed ceiling bounds traversal; it is not an immutable snapshot of a live capture. Concurrent replacement can move a row beyond that ceiling, and eviction can remove earlier records. JSON reports capture_changed, gap, evicted and partial; CSV carries gap, change and eviction columns. The browser rejects a nonadvancing continuation cursor, escapes CSV cells and protects formula-leading text. For frozen retained history, stop monitoring before export; even then the capture remains subject to its expiry/session-retention limits.

Validation boundaries

Status tests cover selection, generation fencing, concurrent attempts, observer failures, no-I/O reads, resume-last and login/CSRF. Timeline tests cover bounded buffers, attribution, rates, owner isolation, expiry, protocol gaps, clock alignment, shared samplers and subprocess cleanup. Their HTTP responses and GPU commands are simulated. Token tests exercise recognized numerical fields and malformed optional metadata.

The review of browser ownership, polling and export paths is based on source; these diagrams do not claim a live GPU, distributed deployment or interactive browser acceptance run. Theme and tooltip work remains outside this refresh.
